---
title: "Beijing: reproduce the saved traffic-map figures"
output: html_document
params:
  snapshot: "../../data/Beijing Data/processed/beijing-visualization.json.gz"
---

This tutorial reproduces the **data layers** in the existing Beijing traffic
visualization using `bdynets`. The standalone dataset was extracted losslessly from the HTML. It contains 288 five-minute frames,
matched road polylines and rounded relative-load values. It is the actual
repository visualization dataset, not a synthetic example. Raw trajectory files
are not required. No model is fitted and no JavaScript or network request runs.

## Read and inspect the standalone saved data

Install `bdynets` from the repository package subdirectory and install `jsonlite`
if needed. Rendering this tutorial additionally requires `rmarkdown` and `knitr`.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(bdynets)
snapshot <- read_traffic_data(params$snapshot)
data.frame(edges=length(snapshot$ids), frames=length(snapshot$bins),
           minutes_per_frame=snapshot$bin_minutes)
snapshot$provenance
```

The source metric is `x_ijt / estimated capacity`; it is **relative load**, not
an observed accident count or a probability. Values are preserved at the HTML's
saved precision. An edge absent from a frame follows the original viewer's zero
convention. That convention belongs to this visualization export and must not
be generalized to missing observations in other datasets.

## Reproduce the three views

Frame 107 is 08:50–08:55 (R indexing starts at one). It has the highest saved
mean relative load and highest saved count of high-load edges. This is a
transparent descriptive selection, not evidence about a model's performance.
The shared package workflow below is also called by `run.R`.

```{r reproduce, fig.width=9, fig.height=7}
frames <- traffic_figures(params$snapshot, "beijing", time_index=107L)
```

The first map uses the source's 0%, 20%, 40%, 60% and 80%+ classes. Gray roads
have zero displayed load. The second map uses red for increases and blue for
decreases relative to the preceding five-minute frame; width represents change
magnitude. The third shows consecutive time above the viewer's 80% threshold,
using the **saved duration records**, with bins converted to minutes.

Matched road polylines and Web Mercator projection are retained. These are
static data-layer reproductions: remote OpenStreetMap tiles, place labels and
browser controls are omitted. Line widths are adapted to a static graphics
device. The figures are therefore not pixel-identical screenshots.

## Select another frame or export publication assets

```{r selected-frame, eval=FALSE}
frame <- traffic_frame(snapshot, time_index=97L, mode="current")
plot(frame) # 08:00–08:05
traffic_figures(params$snapshot, "beijing", time_index=97L,
                output_dir="output/beijing-0800")
```

The export writes PDF and PNG figures, a source-file MD5/selection record and
session information. Existing named outputs are refused. To reuse these data
for inference, obtain the underlying counts and exposure: rounded ratios are
not valid substitutes for count responses.

```{r summary}
frames$current$summary
sessionInfo()
```
